title: Voice from Baghdad
tagline: He broadcast live as bombs fell — the first reporter to cover a war in real time.

scenes.text: Baghdad, January 16, 1991. The Gulf War begins at 2:38 AM. Bombs fall on the city. Every other Western journalist has been evacuated. Three CNN reporters — Peter Arnett, Bernard Shaw, and John Holliman — are live on air from the ninth floor of the Al-Rashid Hotel.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: We can hear explosions. We can see tracer fire lighting up the sky. The city is not dark — it is lit from below by burning buildings and from above by anti-aircraft guns. Ladies and gentlemen, the air war over Baghdad has begun. We are watching it happen.

challenge.instruction: The other networks' lines have gone dead. Close every relay on CNN's four-wire and keep the voices from the ninth floor on the air.
challenge.fact: Peter Arnett broadcast live from Baghdad for CNN during the Gulf War air campaign on January 17, 1991 — the first time a war had been broadcast live on television. His reports from inside the enemy capital were watched by hundreds of millions worldwide.

scenes.text: Arnett had already won a Pulitzer Prize for his Vietnam coverage — dispatches that showed American audiences the war their government was not showing them. In Baghdad, he did something even more radical: he stayed. While other reporters ran, he kept broadcasting.

scenes.speaker: CNN Producer
scenes.text: Peter, the State Department is pressuring us to pull you out. They say your reports are compromising military operations. What do you want to do?

challenge.instruction: Arnett learned to stay put in Vietnam, filing for the AP while others left. Read one of his Saigon dispatches off the teleprinter, lamp by lamp.
challenge.fact: War journalism transformed how governments prosecute and justify wars. Russell's dispatches triggered military reforms; Adams' photo changed American public opinion on Vietnam; Arnett's Gulf War broadcasts created the first live war on television — watched simultaneously by world leaders and ordinary viewers.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: My job is to report what I see. I'm not here to please the Pentagon or Saddam Hussein. I am here because the people watching CNN deserve to know what a war looks like from the city being bombed. Someone has to be here. I will stay.

challenge.instruction: 'Someone has to be here. I will stay.' Get through the blacked-out city and back to the Al-Rashid with the story.
challenge.fact: Arnett's reports were read by Iraqi censors before broadcast, and CNN told viewers so. His report from a bombed factory that Iraq called a baby-milk plant — the US said it made biological weapons — drew fierce criticism in Washington.

scenes.text: The Gulf War was the first war broadcast live on satellite television. CNN's coverage — anchored by Arnett's voice from Baghdad — permanently changed how the world understands war journalism. It created the template for every embedded reporter and every 24-hour news crisis that followed.

challenge.instruction: The whole world is watching the same broadcast at the same moment. Work out what time Arnett's live reports reach each city.
challenge.fact: Live television journalism from a war zone required split-second decisions: what to broadcast, how to frame it, what to leave out. Arnett's reporting from Baghdad was criticised by the US military as too sympathetic to Iraq and praised by journalists as the only independent witness in the city. Both sides were watching the same broadcast.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: In Vietnam I learned that governments tell you what they want you to believe about war. In Baghdad I learned that if you are in the right place with a microphone, the world watches and cannot look away. That is both the power and the weight of being there.

challenge.instruction: If you are in the right place with a microphone, the world cannot look away. Put Arnett's routine in order so the story gets out — and viewers know what it is.
challenge.fact: In March 1997 Arnett, then with CNN, interviewed Osama bin Laden at a hideout in eastern Afghanistan — bin Laden's first television interview — in which he declared holy war on the United States. Four and a half years later came the attacks of 11 September 2001.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: Steve Jobs and Joël Robuchon are still in the rival's hand; they will come to the board one by one. Follow them, start the Lawsuit where they stand, and fight with Kill mode on. A player with no Great People left is out of the game.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 7 · Conquest. Deploy, move to wherever the rival stands, start the Lawsuit there, and attack with Kill mode on until the rival has no Great People left.
challenge.fact: With Kill mode on, a beaten card is discarded instead of returning to hand. A player with no Great People left, in hand or on the board, is out, and the last player standing wins. A kill won in a Great Person's own stat also counts towards their achievement.
